newsitem.title: UK: World sees experience and continuity in Clinton.
newsitem.headline: World sees experience and continuity in Clinton.

text.p: World leaders on Wednesday hailed President Bill Clinton's re-election, saying it ensured experience and continuity in the crucial U.S. role in international affairs.
Russian President Boris Yeltsin sent a message of congratulation to the man he likes to call "my friend Bill" from his hospital bed, just a day after undergoing major heart surgery.

"We think our work together will be fruitful and will allow us to agree on mutually acceptable decisions that meet the interests of both our countries and the whole world community," said Yeltsin. European leaders said Clinton's re-election guaranteed cooperation from an experienced president. Arab countries expressed hope the U.S. would now swing into action to revive the faltering Middle East peace process.
Asian reaction was also warm, with China seeing enhanced prospects for better relations while Japan looked forward to "world peace and prosperity".

Israel, however, quickly told the Arabs not to expect Clinton to pressure the Jewish state into making peace concessions. Washington's long-time bitter enemy Iran said Clinton's re-election meant the United States would maintain its "interventionist and arrogant" policies. There was silence from Gulf War foe Iraq.
Financial markets joined the applause. European bourses climbed sharply as investors welcomed Clinton's re-election and the Republicans' retaining of their grip on Congress as good news for business.
In Europe, French President Jacques Chirac, British Prime Minister John Major and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl were among the first to congratulate Clinton.
Kohl echoed the views of his European Union colleagues in a message to Clinton: "I am delighted we will be able to continue our close and friendly cooperation in the years ahead."

South African President Nelson Mandela was the first African leader to congratulate Clinton, expressing the hope that his country's relations with Washington would continue to improve through Clinton's second term of office.
Middle East reaction came thick and fast, with the Palestinians leading calls for an increased U.S. role in promoting peace in the region.
"We consider the victory of President Clinton a positive step towards a comprehensive, just and permanent peace in the Middle East," Palestinian Legislative Council speaker Ahmed Korei told Reuters.
"It is high time that the U.S. plays an active role in the peace talks between Palestinians and Israelis and acts as a referee," Korei said.
His words were echoed elsewhere in the region.
"We welcome Mr Clinton's re-election," said Jordanian Information Minister Marwan Muasher. "We think his re-election opens the door for a more active role by the U.S. and we would welcome this."

Some Arabs and Israelis expect that a second-term Clinton, eyeing his place in history rather than another election, will try to lean on right-wing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to carry out peace deals.

But Netanyahu made clear he would not be pressured. "The date of the American elections does not materially change their (Arabs') need and their responsibility to enter negotiations," he told reporters. "No one will do the job for them."
In Asia, a Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman told reporters: "We wish to congratulate President Clinton on his re-election.
"Now, a good opportunity has presented itself for improving and expanding Sino-U.S. relations."
Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto was unstinting in his praise for Clinton's victory, saying he congratulated the president "from the bottom of my heart".
"The people of the United States made a very great choice," Hashimoto told reporters.
"President Clinton's re-election reassures us of world peace and prosperity," said Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda.
Vietnam, for years a fierce enemy of the United States, also welcomed the victory of Clinton, who normalised relations between Washington and Hanoi in 1995.

"On our side, Vietnam hopes the cooperative relationship between Vietnam and the United States will continue to develop for the benefit of the two countries and the benefit of peace, stability, cooperation and development in the region and world," a Foreign Ministry spokesman said.
